newsitem.title: USA: Credit card late payments at record high.
newsitem.headline: Credit card late payments at record high.

text.p: Late payments on credit cards jumped to a record high in the second quarter, the American Bankers Association said Tuesday, blaming the fallout from looser lending standards,
Credit card delinquencies were 3.66 percent of the total number of accounts, a 13 basis point jump from 3.53 percent in the first quarter, the banking association said.
The second-quarter credit card delinquency ratio was the highest since the ABA began collecting data in 1974.
However, the pace of the increase was slower than in the first quarter, when credit card late payments jumped 19 basis points, according to the ABA's Consumer Credit Delinquency Bulletin.
A loan is considered delinquent when it is 30 days or more overdue.
"As expected, credit card late payments are continuing to increase in 1996," said James Chessen, ABA's chief economist.
"The delinquencies being seen today are the result of lending decisions made by banks 18 to 24 months ago," he said in a statement.
Late payments for auto loans made through auto dealers rose to 2.48 percent in the second quarter from 2.13 percent.

That increase help push up the composite ratio of delinquencies for loans. The composite of eight types of consumer instalment loans rose to 2.32 percent at the end of the second quarter from 2.14 percent, ABA said.
Banks are making an effort to tighten loan standards, but it will take time before that is reflected in the delinquency ratios, the ABA said.
"Issuers are cutting back on riskier credit card lending programmes, lowering credit limits, lengthening the time between automatic credit limit increases," Chessen said.
The pace of bank consumer lending was virtually flat with a 0.7 percent increase in the first seven months of this year, the ABA said.
"Although loan demand is still strong, consumer borrowing is likely to slow partly due to higher interest rates and banks' tightening of lending standards," the ABA report said.
"While most of the major consumer loan categories are showing increases in late payments, banks are well-positioned to handle any losses generated by the delinquencies," Chessen said.
